bio.en: Paul Millerd is the author of The Pathless Path: Imagining a New Story for Work and Life, a book that has resonated widely in the tech community for challenging the default career trajectory.
bio.zh: Paul Millerd 是《无路之路》（The Pathless Path）一书的作者，该书因挑战传统默认职业轨迹而在科技圈引发广泛共鸣。

summary.en: Paul reframes the 'default path' of work and life as a script we unconsciously follow, and argues that consciously choosing uncertainty can open a more fulfilling route. He shares how a three-month sabbatical - or even a three-hour weekday reset - can create the space to discover what you actually want, and why founders should embrace offering sabbaticals. The conversation is a practical invitation to question the script and design a life on your own terms.
summary.zh: Paul 将工作与生活的“默认路径”重新定义为一种我们在无意识中遵循的剧本，并主张有意识地选择不确定性，反而能通向更充实的人生。他分享了三个月的休假——甚至只是工作日里三小时的抽离——如何创造出发现真正所求的空间，以及为什么创始人应当乐于提供休假。本期是一份务实的邀请：质疑那套剧本，按自己的方式设计人生。

turns.speaker: Paul Millerd
turns.en: Take three hours during a workday. Has to be during a workday. Block off your schedule, sneak out. People can pull this off. Go for a walk without a destination or do something from your childhood that you used to do all the time. Did you use to play basketball? Did you use to paint? Did you use to play an instrument? And just pay attention. What is emerging? Do you feel bad for sneaking out of work? Where does that bad feeling come from? What does that mean about your definition of work and what work means to you? (00:00:30): A lot of people have never really thought about, why do you work? People say money. Okay, that's fine. But what else? Why? Are you trying to be a good person? Do you see a good person as somebody that works every day? Maybe. These are a lot of scripts people grow up with. You're really just creating this space to get in touch with, how do I actually feel about work? How do I get to know myself more? Are there things that I've lost touch with that really bring me alive?
turns.zh: 找个工作日里的三个小时。必须是工作日。腾出时间溜出去。很多人都能做到这点。去散步，不必有明确的目的地；或者重温童年时期常做的事——你以前爱打篮球吗？爱画画吗？爱演奏乐器吗？然后专注当下。会有什么新的感悟浮现？你会为溜出公司感到内疚吗？这种负罪感从何而来？这又说明你对工作的定义是什么？工作对你意味着什么？（00:00:30）很多人从未认真思考过：你为什么工作？人们会说"为了钱"——好吧，这倒也无可厚非。但还有别的理由吗？比如？你想成为一个好人吗？你认为每天工作的人才算好人吗？或许吧。这些都是人们从小耳濡目染的刻板印象。你真正需要做的，是给自己创造一个空间，深入探究：我对工作的真实感受是什么？我如何更深入地认识自己？有没有被遗忘的兴趣爱好能让我重焕生机？

turns.en: Excited to be here Lenny.

turns.zh: 我更兴奋能邀请到你。你出版了一本叫《无路之路》的书，我手头就有一本。上次听说这本书已经卖出4万多本，我知道这让它跻身畅销书前1%之列，甚至可能位列前0.1%。对于一本书来说，这个销量数字高得惊人。但人们往往不了解这一点。尤其是对于自出版书籍而言，这无疑是巨大的成功。（00:05:02）：我觉得你提到的"默认路径"这个概念很值得探讨。什么是默认路径？

turns.speaker: Paul Millerd
turns.en: Yeah, I think the default path is different for everyone and slightly different in every different culture. It's really the story in your head about what you should do. And most of us have some sort of script that we're living out. This is especially powerful when we're in our late teens and early twenties, right? We're trying to execute a script. (00:05:31): And it can be different in every country. In the US it's sort of like go to college, get good grades, get a good job, make a good salary, buy a house, get married, have a family, things like that. And when it comes to work, the default path is get a job and work continuously for all of adulthood. (00:05:50): And when you opt out of the default path, there aren't really offerings. People have a hard time even contemplating it. You'll trigger insecurities in other people by just existing outside the frame of the default path. And it's the default path in their head of their conception of how the world should work and does work, right? (00:06:15): So a lot of what I explore is what is life beyond the default path, and what are the stories we can use to one, at minimum, feel better about what we're doing? And two, what are the stories we can adopt to thrive?
turns.zh:
是的，我认为默认路径因人而异，每个文化也有细微差别。它实质上是你脑海中关于应该做什么的剧本。我们大多数人都在按照某种既定剧本生活。这在青少年晚期和二十岁出头时尤为明显——我们试图按照既定路径行事。
（00:05:31）：这种路径在不同国家也大相径庭。在美国，人们通常认为：上大学、取得好成绩、找到好工作、赚大钱、买房、结婚、组建家庭等等。就工作而言，默认路径就是找份工作，持续工作到成年。
（00:05:50）：当你选择跳出默认路径时，却没有太多支持选择的资源。人们甚至难以想象这种可能性。你只要存在于默认路径之外，便会引发他人的不安。这源于他们对世界应如何运转的既定认知，对吧？
（00:06:15）：所以我探讨的核心问题是：默认路径之外的生活是怎样的？我们能借助哪些故事，至少让自己对当下所做之事感觉更自在？又能采纳哪些故事来实现自我成长？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I imagine many people listening to this are feeling like, "No way I'm on the default path. I'm doing so many interesting things. I'm doing what I want," but they probably still are on this default path. What are some signs that might tell you that you actually still are on this path, and there's such a new direction you could explore that you haven't explored?
turns.zh: 我能想象很多听众会想：“我才不走默认路径呢，我在做很多有趣的事，我在追随自己的热爱！”但他们可能仍深陷其中。怎样判断自己是否仍在默认路径上，又该如何开拓新方向？

turns.speaker: Paul Millerd
turns.en: Yeah, I think there's nothing wrong with the default path. The difference I would make is, are you conscious about what you're actually doing? What are the costs of your game? What are the trade-offs? What are the implicit contracts are you creating with yourself? A lot of times when people quit their jobs, they forget to fire the manager in their head. They don't realize they can take the afternoon off to spend it with their kids. They've created this implicit contract that Monday through Friday, eight to 10 hours a week you have to work. And that may work for people, but are you actually opting into that, or are you just sort of accepting the default?
turns.zh: 是的，我认为默认路径本身并无过错。但关键在于，你是否清楚自己在做什么？游戏规则的代价是什么？隐性契约是什么？很多离职的人忘记解雇自己脑海中的"经理"。他们没有意识到自己可以下午请假陪伴孩子。他们默认了每周一到周五、每天8到10小时的工作时长。这或许适合某些人，但你是在主动选择这种生活，还是只是被动接受默认路径？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think it's a really important point. It's totally fine to stay on this default path. It's not for everyone to try something totally different. Can you talk a little bit about just how to think about the benefits of that and the trade-offs of, "Okay, this is great, I'm going to stay where I am"?
turns.zh: 我认为这是一个很重要的观点。留在默认路径完全没问题。但并非每个人都必须尝试全然不同的生活。能否谈谈如何思考其中的利弊，以及"好吧，我现在很开心，就继续待在原地"的选择背后的隐性代价？

turns.speaker: Paul Millerd
turns.en: It's interesting. I did not think my book would resonate with people that were firmly in the traditional work role. Full-time jobs, big companies, things like that. But I've had many people reach out that say, "Wow, this sort of loosened the tightness between my identity and my work reality, and loosened it up a little bit. And I'm able to play with it a little more." I had one friend, he said, "From your book, I made a list of the four priorities. Right now I'm getting three of them. And it's helped me become more aware that I'm actually getting these three things that I prioritize. I'm missing the fourth. I'm probably going to have to make a change two years from now. Maybe another role, because I do want to lean into that fourth thing." I think it's really just about remixing your path. My hot take is that we're all on a pathless path. You were at Airbnb. Airbnb, every two years were there was a different company.
turns.zh: 真有意思。我原本以为我的书不会引起那些深深扎根于传统职场角色的人的共鸣——比如全职工作、大公司之类的。但很多读者联系我说："哇，这本书让我的身份与工作现实之间的紧张关系松弛了一些，我能更灵活地应对了。"还有位朋友说："从你的书中，我列出了四个优先事项。现在我能做到其中三个。这让我意识到，自己正在实现这三个优先目标，而第四个目标还缺失。或许两年后我得做出改变，换个角色，因为我确实想专注于第四个目标。" 我认为关键在于重构自己的职业路径。我的观点是，我们都身处一条无路可循的道路上。你曾在爱彼家（Airbnb）工作过，那家公司每两年就会有不同的发展方向。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Absolutely true.
turns.zh: 确实如此。

turns.speaker: Paul Millerd
turns.en: Right? And so we're constantly needing to reinvent and reevaluate. And I think thinking of our lives as this smooth trajectory up this corporate ascent sort of limits the possibilities of our own life. So just acknowledging that we are being disrupted. We all have personal lives where we have relationship challenges, health challenges, external shocks, inflation, things like this, that are changing our reality all the time. (00:09:25): And it sort of sucks that there aren't these comfortable middle class jobs that are growing and abundant. They're shrinking. David Autor, a economist from MIT, has pretty good research on this, and it's just making people a little more unsettled. It sucks, but this is the reality we're living in, especially places like the US becoming super tech heavy. And how do you navigate that? It's hard. Everyone's struggling with their relationship to work.
turns.zh: 对吧？所以我们需要不断自我重塑和重新评估。我认为把人生视为一条顺畅的晋升之路，会限制我们自身的可能性。所以要承认我们正面临各种颠覆。我们的个人生活中，总有关系挑战、健康问题、外部冲击、通货膨胀等因素，不断改变着我们的现实。（00:09:25）可惜的是，没有那些稳定且充裕的中产阶级工作岗位了。它们正在缩减。麻省理工学院的经济学家大卫·奥托尔（David Autor）对此有深入研究，这让人们愈发感到不安。确实令人失望，但这就是我们生活的现实，尤其是在美国这样科技高度发达的地区。如何应对这种局面？这很难。每个人都在为与工作的关系而挣扎。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let's actually talk about the pathless path. You've been kind of touching on various ways of thinking about it. What's the simplest way of thinking about this concept of the pathless path?
turns.zh: 那我们来谈谈无路可循的道路吧。你之前提到了各种思考它的方式。怎样最简单地理解这个无路可循的道路的概念？

turns.speaker: Paul Millerd
turns.en: I really shied away from trying to define it super clearly. I think I have this passage at the beginning of the book that it's like the pathless path is basically a shift away from the default. It's a shift away from not knowing what you're doing as a problem to be solved toward an embrace of uncomfort, discomfort, and uncertainty. (00:10:32): And it's sort of a personal journey of shifting away from operating around scarcity towards operating from a sense of abundance, having faith that things might be okay. And on a path like yours, this is a necessary condition. You have no idea what comes next, because nobody has been on the Lenny path before.
turns.zh: 我刻意避免给出过于明确的定义。我觉得书开头有段文字提到，无路可循的道路本质上是偏离默认路径。它意味着从把不知道自己在做什么视为需要解决的问题，转向接纳不安、焦虑和不确定性。（00:10:32）这是一次个人旅程，从围绕稀缺性运作转向基于充足感运作，怀着事情可能会好起来的信念。对于像你这样的道路来说，这是必要的条件。你根本不知道接下来会发生什么，因为以前从未有人走过莱尼（Lenny）的道路。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: True.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.speaker: Paul Millerd
turns.en: Right? And a lot of us are in this situation. Now if you're an accountant at an accounting firm in your early twenties, maybe there is a track, and you can sort of plan it, and it's pretty legible. But even still, I would argue that developing a relationship with uncertainty, not knowing what's happening, experimenting a little more, it's all of these things in one. And it's sort of my attempt to come up with a better narrative around work. (00:11:27): And it's been pretty cool, because a lot of people are embracing this and now using the term like, "I'm on my pathless path." And it allows people to sort of name it and gives them comfort. (00:11:40): I've had people email me that have been on a path for seven years, and they're like, "This is the first time I actually felt okay about my path," because a lot of what my book is, is an exploration of, why does it feel so weird to do your own thing? Why does it actually feel shameful to leave a full-time job? Which is an aberration in the history of the world.
turns.zh: 是吧？我们很多人都身处这种境地。现在，如果你是一家会计事务所的二十出头的会计师，或许还有一条清晰的职业发展路径，你可以规划得井井有条。但即便如此，我还是认为，要学会与不确定性共处，不去预测未来，多去尝试新事物，这一切构成了我对职场的全新解读。（00:11:27）：这种尝试非常棒，因为很多人都接受了这种理念，现在甚至会用“我在走一条无路的路”来形容它。这让人们能给这种状态命名，也能从中获得慰藉。（00:11:40）：我收到过邮件，内容是有人已经走了七年的弯路，他们写道：‘这是我第一次对自己的道路感到安心’。因为我的书主要探讨的是，为什么做自己想做的事会让人觉得如此怪异？为什么离开全职工作会让人感到羞耻？这在人类历史上都是反常的。

turns.speaker: Lenny

And I want to talk about that. But before we do that, what are some examples of pathless paths people have ended up doing? Something just to make it a little more real of, here's what people have ended up doing with their life.
turns.zh: 我相信现在大家心里最大的疑问是：“这听起来很棒。我也想做自己热爱的工作，从这条既定路径中跳出来。但该怎么做呢？”接下来我想谈谈这个问题。但在深入之前，先看看人们最终选择的无路之路都有哪些例子。让大家更直观地了解，人们最终是如何规划自己的人生的。

turns.speaker: Paul Millerd
turns.en: So I think it ranges from a short sabbatical. And to someone like you or me who are sort of on this path and committed to this creator path, and things like that, there's a huge component of their creator economy. Not the creator economy from a VC perspective of all these startups that are going to save creators, but creators that are actually betting on themselves, finding some deeper satisfaction, a better relationship with work and committing to it. But it also encompasses people that are independent freelancers, that have a stable path, more predictable income than creator economy stuff. And it also includes people that are jumping from job to job. (00:13:16): I also have examples of people that are older. I talk to a lot of people in their fifties. They've solved their financial problems, but they've lost that sense of aliveness. And they're looking to re-inject that, and they need maps of how to approach that, how to think about that, what are the models, things like that. (00:13:37): So yeah, it's a pretty big umbrella. It's a nice way to claim everyone's path, but I think the shared ethic is really a sense of possibility, and opportunity, and optimism.
turns.zh:
所以我认为，无路之路的范围很广。既有短暂的休假，也有像你我这样走在创作者之路上的从业者，还有更多依赖创作者经济的人。这里说的创作者经济，不是指风投视角下那些拯救创作者的初创公司，而是指那些真正为自己下注、从中获得更深层次满足感、与工作建立更良好关系并全身心投入的人。此外，还有独立自由职业者，他们的道路更稳定，收入比创作者经济领域的人更可预测。还有那些频繁跳槽的人。
（00:13:16）：我也有年长者的例子。我和很多五十多岁的人交流过。他们解决了财务问题，但失去了生命力感，他们渴望重新注入这种活力，并且需要找到方法去探索、思考、建立模式等等。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So just to kind of list out some of these end, and I think what's interesting is there's no end to this. It's an endless path to continue discovering. There's actually this quote that I wrote down here that I'll read that I think is a really nice way of thinking about this pathless path. "The goal is not to find a job, make money, build a business, or achieve any other metric. It's to actively and consciously search for the work that you want to keep doing."
turns.zh: 所以简单列举一些例子吧，我觉得最有趣的是，这种探索永无止境。这里有句话我记下了，读起来觉得很棒：“目标不是找工作、赚钱、创业或达成任何其他指标。目标是积极主动地寻找你想持续做下去的工作。”

turns.speaker: Paul Millerd
turns.en: The big shift there, the big shift for me actually, when I left my job, I wanted to run away. I wanted to escape work. I wanted to not work. And I more or less accomplished that. I basically lowered my cost of living in Asia to about 1,000 per month. (00:14:34): But then I started developing this relationship with writing, and creating, and all these things I actually really enjoyed. And I wasn't doing them to be famous or grow a following. I just really liked them and I liked doing it in public, because I was meeting others that were engaging on these ideas. (00:14:52): So the big aha for me was, "Oh, you can design around liking work." The hidden assumption I had around work for the first 32, 33 years of my life was work sucks. You have to figure out how to tolerate it. (00:15:13): And within that frame, try to do your best to enjoy some of it. But ultimately, it's a trade-off of your time. You have to suffer through it. A lot of it is going to suck, and you have to put up with that. (00:15:26): Now, I think I'm very protective of what I do and don't do. This is why it was very easy for me to say no to Penguin. I didn't want to write a second book for them. I want to write a second book the way I did, which was super fun process. Writing a book was one of the most fun things I've ever done in my life. And so I sort of think about protecting them. (00:15:48): And a lot of people are looking for meaning through work in a job shaped container. And I think that's just really hard to find. You can find it for short bursts, but maybe after seven or 10 years, it's just not doing it anymore.
turns.zh: 最大的转变在于，我离开工作岗位时其实很想逃离。想逃避工作。不想工作。后来我基本做到了。我把在亚洲的生活成本降到了每月约1000美元。（00:14:34）但随后我开始与写作、创作建立联系，发现自己真正热爱这些事物。我写作和创作不是为了出名或积累粉丝，而是单纯喜欢这些过程，还乐于在公开场合分享心得，因为能与志同道合的人交流想法。（00:14:52）对我来说，最大的顿悟是：“原来你可以围绕‘喜欢工作’来设计生活。” 在前32、33年的人生里，我默认工作就是件糟心事——必须想办法忍受它，然后尽力享受其中的乐趣。但归根结底，工作就是用时间去交换回报，必须忍受其中的痛苦，承受诸多无奈。（00:15:26）如今我对自己的选择格外谨慎。比如拒绝企鹅出版社的邀请时毫不犹豫。我不想为他们写第二本书，而是想按照自己喜欢的方式创作。写书是我人生中最享受的经历之一，所以我必须守护这份热情。（00:15:48）许多人试图在职场的框架内寻找工作的意义，但这实在太难了。短暂的激情易得，七年、十年后却往往归于平淡。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So let's talk about how to go about finding your pathless path and create the space and opportunity to do this. Because again, a lot of people listening are like, "I have bills to pay. I got kids to take care of. I got a home, I got a mortgage. I can't just go on a sabbatical, explore, travel, and find here I'm going to start a newsletter." So what have you found are ways to enable this exploration without risking everything?
turns.zh: 接下来我们来探讨如何找到属于自己的无路之路，并创造条件和机会去践行它。毕竟很多听众会说："我有账单要付，有孩子要养，有房贷要还。总不能放下一切去休假、探索、旅行，然后突然决定开通一个订阅号。"那么，你找到过哪些既能探索未知又不必孤注一掷的方法呢？

turns.speaker: Paul Millerd
turns.en: A three month sabbatical is much more attainable than people think. Companies are desperate to keep people and are much more open to things like this these days. And the way I frame it is if you're assuming you're going to work continuously in adulthood, that's about 500 months. Try to find three months of that where you can create space and reconnect with yourself, explore things, just see what emerges, see how you feel. I think this is so vital for people in their thirties or forties who've worked for 10 years just to reconnect with themselves. (00:17:11): And three months in a total of 500 months, people accomplish much more impressive things than that, like saving for their dream home. That is such a powerful thing people aim for that they make it happen. Even people that don't have a ton are able to make that happen, because it is such an important priority. And for me, I think creating this space was more important than owning a house, getting married. It was the most important thing for me. (00:17:42): And I actually quoted your piece. I pulled up the quote. It said, "Lenny Rachitsky took a sabbatical after a long career in product management, thought he would return to work. But by the end of the break, it was crystal clear to me that I was ready to move on to a new adventure." And then you said several weeks into your sabbatical, you stopped checking your email. "My heart was no longer in the work. I didn't yet know what I wanted to do next, but I knew it was time to shake things up." And you probably weren't in that state when you were still at Airbnb.
turns.zh: 一次为期三个月的休假比人们想象的要容易实现得多。如今，企业迫切希望留住人才，对这类休假安排也更加开放。我的理解是，如果你认为自己成年后会一直工作，那么人生总共约有500个月的时光。试着从中抽出三个月来为自己创造空间、重新与自己连接、探索未知、观察生命的绽放，感受内心的变化。对于那些工作十年却渴望重新认识自己的三四十岁人群来说，这尤为重要。（00:17:11）而在总共500个月的时光里，三个月的休假能成就比这更了不起的事，比如为梦想家园存钱。这种为了达成目标而全力以赴的精神，真的很令人钦佩。即使手头不宽裕的人也能做到，因为这是一个至关重要的优先事项。对我而言，创造这样的空间比买房、结婚更重要。（00:17:42）我还引用了你的一段话。我翻出了那段文字：“莱尼·拉奇茨基在产品管理领域深耕多年后，本以为会重返职场。但休假结束时，他清楚地意识到，自己已准备好开启新的征程。” 你还提到，在休假几周后，你停止了查看邮件。“我对工作的热情已然消退。虽然尚不确定未来的方向，但我知道是时候做出改变了。” 而在Airbnb工作时，你大概还没有这样的状态。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's right. I was super into the work. And I think the way I thought about it is the Kool-Aid kind of exited my bloodstream, and taking that time off kind of created separation. And then I started thinking, "Man, is this really what I want to be doing?" And that visceral feeling of getting excited about the work disappeared, which was crazy and scary.
turns.zh: 确实如此。当时我完全沉浸在工作中。我觉得当时的状态就像是被洗脑了一样，休假让一切变得清晰明了。然后我开始反思：“天啊，这真的是我想要的生活吗？” 那种对工作的狂热感消失了，这既令人惊讶又令人恐惧。

turns.speaker: Paul Millerd
turns.en: Yeah. And so you have smart listeners, and smart people are great at excuses. So they'll say, "I can't do it because of this." I always think these things are much more possible if they really are the main priority. (00:18:48): So what I tell people is fine, don't take a sabbatical. Take an afternoon. Take three hours during a workday. Has to be during a workday. Block off your schedule, sneak out. People can pull this off. Go for a walk without a destination, or do something from your childhood that you used to do all the time. Did you use to play basketball? Did you use to paint? Did you use to play an instrument? Do one of those two things, even better if you do both. (00:19:19): And just pay attention. It's a sort of form of work mindfulness. What is emerging? Do you feel bad for sneaking out of work? Where does that bad feeling come from? What does that mean about your definition of work and what work means to you? (00:19:38): A lot of people have never really thought about, why do you work? People say money. Okay, that's fine. But what else? Why do you work? Are you trying to be a good person? Do you see a good person as somebody that works every day? Maybe. These are a lot of scripts people grow up with. Or people that don't have a full-time job, are they bad people? (00:20:04): And so you're really just creating this space to get in touch with, how do I actually feel about work? How do I get to know myself more? Are there things that I've lost touch with that really bring me alive?
turns.zh: 是的。所以你有聪明的听众，而聪明的人总能找到各种借口。比如他们会说：“我做不到，因为这样那样的原因。” 我总觉得，如果某件事真是你的首要任务，那它就更有可能实现。（00:18:48）所以我给人们的建议是，不用休长假。抽个下午，利用工作日里的三个小时。必须是在工作日。安排好日程，偷偷溜出去。人们完全能做到这一点。去散散步，不必有明确的目的地，或者做些童年时期常做的事。你以前打篮球吗？画画吗？弹乐器吗？选其中一项，最好两项都尝试。（00:19:19）然后专注当下。这是一种工作中的专注力。有什么新发现？偷偷溜出办公室工作会让你感觉内疚吗？这种负罪感从何而来？这说明你对工作的定义是什么，工作对你的意义又是什么？（00:19:38）很多人从未真正思考过：你为什么工作？人们会说：为了钱。好吧，这没问题。但还有别的吗？你为什么工作？你是在努力做个好人吗？你认为每天工作的人才是好人吗？或许吧。这是人们从小就耳熟能详的观念。或者那些没有全职工作的人，他们就是坏人吗？（00:20:04）所以你其实是在创造一个空间，让自己去感知：我对工作的真实感受是什么？我如何能更了解自己？有没有被遗忘却能真正让我充满活力的事物？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's interesting how much of what you described, we didn't know each other before we met for this podcast episode, but so much of what you say is exactly what happened in my path. I took three months off exactly. I took a sabbatical. I started poking around, exploring, doing a little writing. And basically led to what I do now, which is a crazy thing I never imagined in my wildest dreams. And so clearly this works.
turns.zh: 有趣的是，你描述的很多内容，我们在做这期播客之前并不相识，但你说的很多事恰恰就是我人生路上的经历。我休了整整三个月的假。我休了sabbatical。我开始四处探索、写作。最终成就了现在的事业——这简直是我做梦都想不到的疯狂转变。所以显然这种方法确实有效。

turns.speaker: Paul Millerd
turns.en: Yeah, and I think people will say, "You can do that because you worked at Airbnb," or, "Oh, you can do that because you"... I've talked to hundreds of people. So what I did before the pandemic for years was I opened up my calendar every Wednesday and I said, anyone that wants to talk to me about work can talk to me about work. (00:21:02): So at this point, I've probably talked to 500 plus people about their relationship to work. And the reason that's not surprising about what happened to you is it happens to almost everyone. The sabbatical almost has a 99.9% approval rating. (00:21:22): I talked to one person. She was like, "I took a sabbatical, I stayed at home. My husband was still working for two months. I couldn't wait to go back to work." I was like, "Cool. You're the first person I met that didn't get anything out of a sabbatical."
turns.zh: 是啊，我想人们会说：“你能做到是因为你在Airbnb工作过”，或者“哦，你能做到是因为你……”我和数百人聊过天。在疫情前，我多年来每周三都会开放日程，告诉所有想和我谈工作的人，都可以来谈工作。（00:21:02）到现在，我大概和500多人聊过他们与工作的关系。你的经历并不令人惊讶，因为这种情况几乎发生在每个人身上。sabbatical几乎有99.9%的成功率。（00:21:22）我遇到过一个人。她说：“我休了sabbatical，待在家里。我丈夫还在工作两个月。我迫不及待想回去工作。” 我说：“酷啊。你是我遇到的第一个从sabbatical中毫无收获的人。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's hilarious. I haven't met that person. So your advice is try to take a sabbatical, and you're also encouraging people to, you can actually probably do this at some point, but maybe it takes a bit of time to set people up for the fact that you're going to do this. Maybe you need to work at the company for a while, but in your thirties or forties, it sounds like try to find time to take three months. And is three months important? Is that what you find, that large of a block of time?
turns.zh: 太搞笑了。我还没遇到过那样的人。所以你的建议是尝试休sabbatical，同时你也在鼓励人们，或许人们确实能在某个时候做到，但可能需要一些时间让大家做好心理准备。比如在三四十岁时，试着找时间休三个月。三个月重要吗？你发现这段时间足够长吗？

turns.speaker: Paul Millerd
turns.en: I've found it takes six to eight weeks just to unwind.
turns.zh: 我发现光是放松下来就需要六到八周的时间。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, that's exactly what I found.
turns.zh: 是啊，这正是我发现的情况。

turns.speaker: Paul Millerd
turns.en: I think for me, there was the initial unwinding after six to eight weeks, and then a deeper unwinding after probably two to three years, where you start to trust yourself a little more, if you stay on the uncertain path that is. But yeah.
turns.zh: 我觉得对我来说，最初的放松是在六到八周后，而更深层的放松可能要等两到三年后——在这期间，你会更信任自己，只要你坚持走这条不确定的道路。但确实如此。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: If founders are listening to this and feeling like, "Shit, why would I give people sabbaticals? They're going to leave, start their own companies, find some other catalyst path. I want them on my default path." Is there anything you could say to a founder thinking about offering sabbatical?
turns.zh: 如果有创业者听了这段话后觉得，"天啊，我为什么要给员工休假？他们会离开公司，自己创业，寻找其他发展机会。我希望他们能走我设定的常规路线。" 对于考虑提供休假计划的创业者，你有什么建议吗？

turns.speaker: Paul Millerd
turns.en: I would say if that's their reaction, it sounds like they have an insecurity around work. So I would interrogate that first. What is the implicit story they have about how much people are supposed to work and such? (00:23:00): Yeah, I don't know if it's a good employer strategy. I think a decent amount of people would leave. I know Intel, I have friends that have done the sabbatical at Intel. You get six weeks after seven years. Maybe after seven years, they're a bit burnt out that they don't have enough time in those six weeks to unwind. (00:23:22): But I think getting creative, especially now that remote work is so much more common about these opportunities, to let people become the people they want to be. People leave companies because they don't see a path to be the person they want to be.
turns.zh: 我会说，如果他们的反应是这样，说明他们对工作存在不安全感。首先我会探究这个问题。他们对员工应该工作多少时间的隐含观念是什么？（00:23:00）：嗯，我不确定这是否是个好的雇主策略。我觉得会有相当多的人离开公司。我了解英特尔，我有朋友在那里休过假。员工工作七年后才能获得六周休假。可能七年后，他们已经精疲力竭，以至于这六周根本没时间放松。（00:23:22）但我认为要发挥创造力，尤其是在远程工作越来越普遍的今天，创造机会让人们成为自己想成为的人。人们离开公司往往是因为看不到一条通往理想自我的路径。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, so you take a sabbatical, or you take an afternoon, or you take a walk. You talked about be mindful for what comes up. What are you feeling about work? What is a thing you want to do? Do you want to go play basketball? Do you want to go draw? What else do you encourage people to do, to try to discover a potential new path?
turns.zh: 好的，你可以休假、抽个下午休息，或者去散步。你谈到要留意出现的想法。那么你对工作的感受是什么？你想做什么？你想去打篮球吗？你想去画画吗？你还鼓励人们做些什么来探索新的发展路径？

turns.speaker: Paul Millerd
turns.en: I think meeting others. So in exercise, I'll have people do if they're curious about this... And for the most part, I don't want to convert people that like what they're doing and like traditional jobs. But a lot of people are curious, and I say have a path expert conversation. Reach out to somebody, sort of like a podcast, that's ahead of you on a similar path, and just send them a message and say, really thoughtful message. Say, "Hey, you're on a path a few years ahead of me. I'm really curious about this. I don't have people in my life that have done things like this. Can I just pick your brain? If we can't jump on a call, can I send you a list of questions?" (00:24:42): Most people will agree to that, especially the latter if they're a writer, because writing just enables them to come up with new ideas. So I'll always agree to do the written questions. I don't do the open calendar anymore now that I have a daughter. She wins my time over random stranger's booking. But if people want to send me questions, I'll always answer them in text form.
turns.zh: 我觉得是多与他人交流。比如在我的实践中，我会让感兴趣的人去做……大多数情况下，我不想改变那些热爱现有工作、喜欢传统职位的人。但很多人很好奇，我会建议他们和路径专家交流。联系一个在相似道路上领先你几年，且有相关经验的人，比如播客嘉宾，发一条深思熟虑的消息。比如，“嘿，你比我领先几年的路径让我很着迷。我身边没有做过类似事的人。我能请教下你的经验吗？如果不能通话，能否发送问题列表？”（00:24:42）大多数人都会同意，尤其是后者，如果他们是作家的话，因为写作能激发他们的新想法。所以我总是愿意接受书面提问。但现在有女儿后，我就不再接受公开日程安排了。女儿更需要我的时间，而不是随机的陌生人邀约。但如果有人想发送问题，我会一直以文字形式回复。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And again, this path doesn't have to lead to creator, artist, writer person. It could lead to starting a new business. It could probably lead to a new career. It could shift in careers. Is there anything else, again, of just where this could lead to people so they're like, "Oh, wow, that's interesting."
turns.zh: 再说一次，这条路不一定要通向创作者、艺术家或作家。它可能通向创办新公司，也可能通向转行，甚至是职业转变。还有其他可能吗？让人们能感叹“哦，哇，这真有趣。”

turns.speaker: Paul Millerd
turns.en: Somebody sent me an article today about this guy. I think he was a performing artist. He became a therapist. I forget his name. But I think just the possibilities for reinventing yourself and taking different paths, working online, working flexibly, it's way more possible than 25 years ago. It's also going to continue to be more possible. All the tools and technology to enable these kinds of lives are just getting better and easier. And especially this week, ChatGPT just released their new GPT. I was playing with that today and I'm like, "Oh my gosh."
turns.zh: 有人今天给我发了一篇关于这个人的文章。我觉得他之前是个表演艺人，后来转行做了心理治疗师。我忘了他的名字。不过我觉得，自我重塑、尝试不同发展路径、远程办公、灵活工作等可能性，如今比25年前要大得多，而且这种趋势还会持续下去。支持这些生活方式的工具和技术正变得越来越先进、越来越易用。特别是这周，ChatGPT刚刚发布了新版GPT。我今天试用了一下，简直惊叹不已。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This episode is brought to you by Wix Studio. Your agency has just landed a dream client, and you already have big ideas for the website, but do you have the tools to bring your ambitious vision to life? Let me tell you about Wix Studio, the new platform that lets agencies deliver exceptional client sites with maximum efficiency. How? (00:26:22): First, let's talk about advanced design capabilities. With Wix Studio, you can build unique layouts with a revolutionary grid experience, and watches elements scale proportionally by default. No-code animations at sparks of delight, while adding custom CSS gives total design control. Bring ambitious client projects to life with any industry, with a fully integrated suite of business solutions. From e-commerce to events, bookings, and more. And extend the capabilities even further with hundreds of APIs and integrations. (00:26:50): You know what else? The workflows just make sense. There's the built-in AI tools, the on canvas collaborating, a centralized workspace, the reuse of assets across sites, the seamless client handover, and that's not all. Find out more at wix.com/studio. (00:27:08): I think when people might hear some of these professions like, "Maybe I'll become a therapist, maybe I'll become an online writer person. Maybe I'll start a business." It may feel like that assumes you'll make less money doing these things. But in my case, and I'm curious if it's in your case, I make significantly more doing what I do now. I try not to talk about the income of this stuff, but it's significantly more than I made at Airbnb as a very senior product leader. And I feel like that often happens. You discover a way to do something you love and also make a lot more money.
turns.zh: 本期节目由Wix Studio赞助。你的团队刚刚接手了一个理想客户，你已经对网站设计有了宏伟构想，但你是否有工具来实现这些远大愿景？让我为你介绍Wix Studio这个新平台，它能助力创意机构以最高效率为客户打造卓越网站。如何做到？（00:26:22）：首先，谈谈先进的设计功能。借助Wix Studio，你可以通过革命性的网格体验构建独特布局，元素默认按比例缩放。无代码动画能带来惊喜效果，同时自定义CSS让设计完全可控。无论是何种行业，都能为客户打造出色的项目，平台还集成了电商、活动、预订等全套商业解决方案。通过数百个API和集成功能，功能可进一步扩展。（00:26:50）：还有一点很棒，工作流程非常合理。内置AI工具、画布协作、集中式工作区、跨站资产复用、无缝交接客户等功能一应俱全。欲了解更多信息，请访问wix.com/studio。（00:27:08）：我觉得当人们听到一些职业时，比如“或许我会成为心理治疗师，或许会成为在线作家。或许会创业。”，他们可能觉得这些职业收入会较低。但就我而言，我现在做的事情收入比在Airbnb担任高级产品负责人时高得多。我尽量不谈论这些收入数字，但确实比那时高很多。我发现这种情况经常出现——你找到一种既能做自己热爱之事，又能赚大钱的方式。

turns.speaker: Paul Millerd
turns.en: I think it's easier to make money in a sustainable, long-term way doing stuff you actually like doing. That sounds so simple, but it actually would've been really hard for me to stay on my previous path. (00:27:53): Now, in my case, it was not until my fifth year that I came close to the salary I left. For the first three years, I really optimized for exploration, creativity, just getting to know myself again. I made 50 grand the first year, because I was freelancing. Then I made 30 grand, 24 grand, and then 30 grand. So I was really optimizing for getting to know myself. I dramatically lowered my cost of living, and that is one path. (00:28:26): But this year, I'll make more than I ever made. And that is mind-blowing to me, because every single day of this year has been absolutely delightful. I've spent abundant time with my wife and my daughter. And it's so crazy. (00:28:44): Now, if I had stayed in my previous path, I'd be making a lot more than I make now. But that path was not viable for me for becoming... I'd be so frustrated right now if I had to go back to work. An eight-month-old, I know you have a four-month-old. Wait till eight months old. They're so fun to hang out with.
turns.zh: 我认为，如果你能做自己真正喜欢的事情，以可持续、长期的方式赚钱会更容易。这听起来很简单，但对我来说，坚持走之前的路线其实会非常困难。（00:27:53）：就我个人而言，直到第五年，我才接近我离开前的那份薪资水平。前三年，我主要专注于探索、创造，重新认识自己。第一年我做自由职业，赚了5万美元；第二年赚了3万美元，第三年赚了2.4万美元，第四年又赚了3万美元。所以我当时主要在优化自己，重新认识自己。我大幅降低了生活成本，这是一条路径。（00:28:26）：但今年我的收入会比以往任何一年都高。这让我很惊喜，因为今年的每一天都过得非常愉快。我和妻子、女儿共度了大量时光，真是太棒了。（00:28:44）：如果我继续走之前的路线，现在赚的钱会更多得多。但那条路线对我来说是不可行的，因为我现在回头看，如果不得不回去工作，我会非常沮丧。八个月大的孩子，我知道你家孩子才四个月。等孩子八个月大再说吧。他们真的很可爱，陪他们玩耍真是太有趣了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I can't wait. You talked about this lower spend, lower expense life. What other tips and tricks do you have for people to create this space where they can continue living and paying the rent, while exploring, and wandering, and exploring these things? Is it cut down on expenses? Is there anything else that one can do?
turns.zh: 我迫不及待想听听你说的降低生活成本、优化开支的生活方式。除了削减开支，还有什么其他技巧或方法，能让人创造出既能维持生计、又能探索未知的空间呢？

turns.speaker: Paul Millerd
turns.en: I've talked to so many people at this point. I've seen all sorts of things. I've seen people move abroad. I've seen families with kids and a mortgage sell their house and decide to live in an RV. I've seen people dip into their retirement. I've seen people apply for grants and get those. I've seen people apply for loans. (00:29:55): A big move that a lot of people do is turn their current job into a contract job, which a lot of employers are a lot more open than people would think. Because a contractor's very easy to fire. You can fire a contractor in a day. So if the company's struggling, boom, you're gone, right? (00:30:14): And so there is more risk, but if you're known in the company, it can actually be a somewhat stable path to create more space in your life. You say, "Hey, I want to work three days a week. I want to be a contractor. Here's exactly what I want to do. Are you open to this?" (00:30:30): And as soon as you're a contractor, they can't tell you where to work. You can develop a relationship and they can ask you to work in a certain place, but they don't have control over where you work.
turns.zh: 到目前为止，我和很多人交流过，也见证了各种各样的生活方式。比如有人移居海外，有孩子又背负房贷的家庭卖掉房子，住进房车；有人动用退休金申请助学金，贷款等等。（00:29:55）：很多人会采取的一个重大转变是把现有工作转为合同工，许多雇主对此比人们想象的要开放得多，因为解雇合同工要容易得多。公司如果经营困难，第二天就能把你裁掉，对吧？（00:30:14）：这种转变有更高的风险，但如果你在公司里比较受欢迎，这其实可以成为一种相对稳定的途径，让生活更有弹性。你可以说：“嘿，我想每周工作三天，当个合同工。我想做这个项目。你能接受吗？”（00:30:30）：一旦成为合同工，公司就无法规定你的工作地点了。你可以建立合作关系，他们可能会要求你去某个地方工作，但无法控制你的工作地点。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: A trick that I found really useful actually for helping me feel comfortable about taking time off, I ended up taking six months off, and then it ended up being a year off because I kept trying to figure out what is the thing I wanted to do. The way that I felt good about that is I set a budget of, "Here's the runway that I'm going to give myself. Here's how much it's going to cost to do this for six months. Here's the runway I'm going to give myself. I'm just going to burn through this money, just with the bet that it'll lead to something interesting." And that made me and my wife also just feel like, okay, we were going to lose all that money probably, but the bet is it's going to lead to something really great.
turns.zh: 我发现一个非常有效的技巧，能帮助我坦然享受休假。我最终休了六个月假，最后又休了一年，因为我一直在探索自己想做什么。让我感觉安心的是，我设定了一个预算：“这是我给自己留出的缓冲期。六个月内做这个事需要多少钱？这是我给自己的缓冲期。我就打算把这笔钱烧光，就赌一把它能带来有趣的机会。”这让我和妻子也觉得，嗯，我们可能会损失所有这笔钱，但赌注是它会带来很棒的机会。

turns.speaker: Paul Millerd
turns.en: Yeah, I love this. I think this is something I've been thinking about a lot lately, and I've actually been trying to write something around this, which is that naming what you're spending money on or coming up with agreements like that, you're sort of saying, "This is money I'm investing in my life MBA." Because if somebody says, "I'm going to Stanford Business School," generally you'll receive positive praise. "Oh, that's awesome." But what they're really doing is not working for two years and spending 150 to $200,000, and not earning a salary. (00:31:55): And then to me, it was really interesting to look back at my path. Now, the first three years of my path, I broke even. But compared to being in business school, people thought business school was way better of a path for me. People were judgmental in my path, critical of my path, insulted me, projected their insecurities on me. "How could you do this? This is so crazy. What's your plan?" So coming up with these reframes is super powerful. (00:32:26): One powerful one that worked for me was consider it a gift from your former self. So on the consulting path, I did like it for a while, but at the end I didn't like it. I was sort of just grinding through, going through the motions. I was good at it, but I really didn't want to be doing it if I had choice. And so I earned a decent income doing it. So would I gift that to my future self to be happier? Yeah. So now that I'm in the present, receive that gift and be like, "Thank you former self for working that job."
turns.zh: 是啊，我太喜欢这个观点了。我觉得这正是我最近一直在深思的问题，而且我也一直在试着围绕这个主题写点东西——那就是，明确自己花钱的用途，或者制定类似的协议，就等于是在说：“这笔钱是我为自己的MBA人生投资的。” 因为如果有人说：“我要去斯坦福商学院”，人们通常会给予赞赏：“哦，太棒了。” 但他们真正在做的是放弃两年的工作机会，花费15万到20万美元，却没有任何收入。（00:31:55）对我来说，回顾自己的过往经历很有意思。最初的三年，我虽然没有亏本，但人们却认为读商学院是更好的选择。人们对我的人生道路充满评判，指责我、贬低我，甚至把自己的不安投射到我身上。他们会说：“你怎么能这么做？太疯狂了。你有什么计划？” 所以，重新构建思维模式真的非常有效。（00:32:26）对我有效的一个方法是，把这看作是自己过去的礼物。在咨询行业，我一开始还挺喜欢，但最后却不喜欢了。那时我只是在机械地重复工作，虽然做得不错，但如果可以选择，我根本不想继续下去。不过我确实赚了不少钱。那么，我会把这份礼物送给未来的自己，让他过得更快乐吗？会的。现在我回过头来，接收这份礼物，然后说：“谢谢过去的自己，谢谢你做过那份工作。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's interesting. I could also flip it from the other way of your future self is returning to, "Hey, here's some money to spend to help become who I've become."
turns.zh: 这很有趣。我还能反过来，想象未来的自己回馈给你：“嘿，这里有一些钱，可以用来帮助你成为现在的自己。”

turns.speaker: Paul Millerd
turns.en: Yeah, exactly.
turns.zh: 是啊，没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So I imagine not everyone ends up on a beautiful, amazing new life. They go down this route, they spend a bunch of money, and then they're like, "God damn, I don't have anything to show for it. I've spent all this cash." Imagine there are stories of that. Is there anything you could share around those stories and how to maybe either avoid them or be okay with them?
turns.zh: 所以我想，并非每个人都能迎来美好的新生活。他们走上这条路，花了大笔钱，然后却说：“天哪，我一无所获。这些钱都白花了。” 想象一下有这样的故事。关于这些故事，以及如何避免或坦然面对，你能分享些心得吗？

turns.speaker: Paul Millerd
turns.en: I think there are surprisingly few stories of that. I think that is people's fear of what might happen. What I've seen in reality, as soon as people are without an income or without a job, they spur into action. People, we're far more creative than we give ourselves credit for. Having a child, we have no idea what we're doing when they come out. (00:34:03): But it makes perfect sense that you're going to figure everything out, because you have to. You have no choice. And so the ingenuity and creativity of people as soon as they bet on themselves and go off into the wilderness, is far more than people expect. (00:34:24): And it also has to do with regrets. People do not regret the things they do. They regret the things they didn't do. And the reason for this is if you've made a mistake, you can actually take action to correct it. But if you didn't do the thing that you're regretting, there's nothing you can do except do the thing.
turns.zh: 我觉得这类故事少得惊人。人们往往害怕未知的结果。但现实中，我发现一旦人们失去收入或工作，他们就会立即行动起来。人们远比自己想象的更有创造力。比如养孩子时，我们对如何做父母一无所知。（00:34:03）但很自然地，你会找到解决办法，因为你必须这样做，没有选择余地。一旦人们相信自己，放手去闯，展现的创造力远超预期。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And it reminds me of a quote that you have in your book that I have here. The secret to doing good research, and I think it's related to this of finding a new path, a pathless path, is always to be a little underemployed. You waste years by not being able to waste hours.
turns.zh: 这让我想起你书中的一句话：做好研究的秘诀——我认为这与寻找新路径、无路之路有关——就是始终保持适当的「低就业」状态。人们会浪费数年时间，却不愿浪费几个小时。

turns.speaker: Paul Millerd
turns.en: Yeah. And I wonder if you've found this too. Sometimes, the best way for me to write is to go for a walk, or to take a couple days off and just sort of reset. Creative work can't be forced a lot of time. (00:35:20): And increasingly, a lot of work is creative work. Your work at Airbnb was ultimately creative work. You're creating new products and offerings, in a whole new conception of an industry. You're making stuff up. A lot of times, I think people get fried in these companies because they're not actually given the schedules and the support systems around what actually enables creativity.
turns.zh: 是啊，我想你可能也有过类似的体会。有时候，对我来说，最好的写作方式就是去散散步，或者休息几天，让思绪重新活络起来。创造性工作往往不能强行推进。（00:35:20）如今，越来越多的工作都需要创造力。你在Airbnb的工作本质上就是创造性工作——你正在创造新产品和新服务，重构整个行业的认知体系。你在开创全新的事物。很多时候，我觉得人们在这些公司里精疲力竭，往往是因为他们没有得到真正支持创造力的日程安排和配套体系。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, absolutely. Although I find with writing also, there's the benefit of the opposite of, "I'm just going to sit here and write, and I'm not going to give myself a chance to go walk around. I'm just going to keep writing, even if it's terrible, because it'll maybe lead to something."
turns.zh: 是啊，确实如此。不过我发现写作也有个相反的益处：你不会只坐着写，不给自己机会出去走走。即便写得糟糕，你也会坚持下去，因为说不定能因此获得灵感。

turns.speaker: Paul Millerd
turns.en: Yeah. And even that though, a lot of times, what ends up on the page surprises you. Right? So you do need a certain sense of openness to let that emerge.
turns.zh: 是啊。但即便如此，写在纸上的内容往往会让你感到惊喜，对吧？所以你确实需要保持开放的心态，让灵感自然涌现。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So kind of along the same lines, another important concept that you talk about in your book for finding this pathless path is just this idea that it's not ever like this all or nothing. I'm just going to leap into this new thing. It's kind of this, the way you put it is people quit jobs after years of awakening and safely testing changes, kind of eliminating risks along the way.
turns.zh: 顺着这个思路，你在书中提到的另一个重要概念——找到这条无路之路——就是不要总是一味追求全有或全无。不要一股脑儿扎进新事物。用你书中的话说，就是人们在觉醒并安全测试变革、逐步消除风险多年后，才毅然辞职。

turns.speaker: Paul Millerd
turns.en: So years before I left, and I'm curious if you had a similar experience, I was starting to read personal development books. I was reading Tim Ferriss. I was doing these small experiments like coaching on the side, helping people with their resumes, volunteering, helping people with careers. (00:37:00): And so I was writing too. I was writing for fun on Quora with no goals. And all these things make perfect sense now. And even looking back further, I was always tinkering on the internet, and all these things fit my story perfectly now. (00:37:16): But I didn't know why I was doing them at the time. But each one gave me the confidence to be like, "Okay, I don't love my day job, but all these random things I'm doing on the side, like writing an article and posting it on Medium and LinkedIn, and the people I'm meeting, this is really interesting and energizing. I'm going to pay attention to that energy. Something is there." (00:37:41): And when I quit my job, I didn't really have a plan for how to deal with that, but I had experienced enough of this positive energy. I was like, "I want to chase that. I want to go after that."
turns.zh: 在我辞职前几年，我也有过类似经历。我开始读个人发展类书籍，比如蒂姆·费里斯（Tim Ferriss）的作品。我尝试了一些小实验，比如兼职做职业指导，帮人修改简历，参与志愿服务，帮助别人规划职业生涯。（00:37:00）那时我也在写作，在Quora上写写乐趣文章，没有任何目标。现在回想起来，一切都顺理成章。甚至更早的经历——我总是在网上折腾各种小玩意儿——也完美契合了我的发展轨迹。（00:37:16）但当时我并不知道为什么要这么做。不过每一次尝试都让我更有信心：好吧，我不喜欢现在的工作，但这些业余尝试，比如写篇文章发到Medium和领英上，还有结识的那些人，这些都让我兴致盎然、充满活力。我要关注这种能量，肯定有其意义。（00:37:41）辞职时，我并没有明确的计划，但我已经积累了足够的正能量。我想，既然如此，那就追随它吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's exactly what I found. So I'll tell my story briefly on this. Some advice I got when I went on my sabbatical that ended up being incredibly powerful is essentially what you just said, which is when you're doing stuff during some period of time off, pay really close attention to what gives you energy after you do the thing. Say you have a call. Did that give you energy or did that sap you of energy? Do you feel more energized or you feel like, "I'm tired now"? (00:38:19): So it's like after calls you make, after things you do with friends, after some kind of hobby you're trying to do, after you write some stuff, just pay really close attention to what energizes you, what saps you energy. And then my whole strategy was just do more of the things that energize me and do less of the things that de-energize me. (00:38:37): So in my case, I thought I'd want to do some advising or consulting. I found after every advising call, I was de-energized. I was just like, "No, I do not enjoy this as much as I thought." But after writing and putting a piece out, I was like, "Wow, this is really cool." Even though writing's very hard and there's a lot of de-energized moments, broadly it's like, "Wow, this is cool. People seem to really value this." So I started doing that more. I thought I wanted to start a company, but that kept sucking me of energy as I was working on ideas. So that alone was really, really powerful. And it sounds like really simple advice, but it's really [inaudible 00:39:10].
turns.zh: 没错，我正是发现了这一点。所以我要简要分享一下我的经历。我休假期间得到的一条极其有效的建议，基本上就是你刚刚提到的——当你在休假期间做某件事时，要密切留意哪些事能给你能量，哪些事会消耗你的能量。比如接到一个电话后，是让你精力充沛还是感到疲惫？写作之后，你会感觉更有活力还是觉得“现在好累”？（00:38:19）所以在通话结束后、与朋友共度时光后、尝试新爱好后、完成写作后，都要仔细观察哪些事能给你能量，哪些事会消耗你的能量。然后我的整个策略就是，多做能给我能量的事，少做消耗能量的事。（00:38:37）以我自己为例，我本想做一些咨询或顾问工作，但每次咨询电话结束后，我都精疲力竭。当时我就在想，“不，我并没有想象中那么喜欢这份工作。”但写作完成并发表后，那种满足感简直难以置信。尽管写作过程很艰难，时常感到精疲力竭，但总体来说还是很棒，人们似乎很重视我的作品。所以我开始投入更多精力在写作上。我原本想创业，但在构思项目时总是耗尽精力。这真的太有力量了。听起来是个很简单的建议，但实施起来却异常困难。

turns.speaker: Paul Millerd
turns.en: It's hard too. I think the pull to create a company when you leave a big tech company is so powerful. And what you're saying is sort of crazy. You're saying, "I just feel good writing. I'm going to follow that."
turns.zh: 这确实很难。我觉得从大科技公司离职后想要创业的冲动太强烈了。而你说的话听起来有点疯狂。你说：“我写作时感觉很棒，我要专注于此。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's not a popular path amongst my friends and family.
turns.zh: 在我的朋友和家人中，这条路并不受欢迎。

turns.speaker: Paul Millerd
turns.en: And I think the root of that is you're triggering insecurities in them. You're doing something they weren't allowed to do at your age.
turns.zh: 我认为根本原因在于你触动了他们的不安全感。你正在做他们这个年龄不被允许做的事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The thing I found really helpful there, another friend gave me this advice, just tell people you're tinkering. When they ask you, "What are you working on?" "I'm just tinkering. I'm tinkering with some writing." Because something about that word makes it sound like, "Okay, cool, it's delightful and cool. Tinker wave."
turns.zh: 我发现有个朋友给我的建议很管用，就是告诉别人你在折腾。当他们问你：“你在忙什么？”你就说：“我在折腾呢，写点东西。”因为这个词能让人感觉：“哦，挺酷的，很有趣，折腾吧。”

turns.speaker: Paul Millerd
turns.en: I feel like that did not work with my parents. But yeah, trying different things. I always tell people you need a boomer compatible story for what you're up to, as just give them something. Just say, "I'm an entrepreneur," or, "I'm a business owner."
turns.zh: 我觉得这招对我父母不管用。但确实要多尝试不同的事。我总是告诉别人，要为你要做的事准备一个“婴儿潮一代能接受的故事”，就是给他们一个说得过去的理由。比如说：“我是个创业者。”或者“我是个企业主。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That totally resonates. I'd be excited about that if I was a boomer. In the book, you also talk about taming fears. So we talked about a few of these things, and just the power of taming some of these fears that you have. There's success, the fear of not being successful, of money, of belonging, of loneliness, and of health. Can you just talk about either all of those or any of those, just why it's important to tame those fears, and then how one goes about taming these fears?
turns.zh: 这点我深有共鸣。如果我是婴儿潮一代，我也会为此感到兴奋。在书中，你还谈到克服恐惧。所以我们聊了几个方面，以及克服这些恐惧的力量。比如成功恐惧、害怕不成功、金钱恐惧、归属感恐惧、孤独恐惧和健康恐惧。你能否谈谈克服这些恐惧的重要性，以及具体的做法？

turns.speaker: Paul Millerd
turns.en: Yeah. So a big source of inspiration around this is Tim Ferriss' fear setting, and he basically forces you to write down what are your fears, how could you mitigate these. But more powerfully, the second part is... And you're framing them around action. And so he reframes, what is the cost of inaction? And that was really powerful for me, and it sort of exposed a lot of the costs in the current state of what I was doing. (00:41:16): And so actually, I want to thank you. It's funny, you messaged me as I was listening to a podcast you were on. I think it was the one with David Perell.
turns.zh: 是的。关于这个主题的一个重要灵感来源是蒂姆·费里斯（Tim Ferriss）的恐惧设定法。他基本上会让你写下自己的恐惧是什么，以及如何减轻这些恐惧。但更重要的是，第二部分是……你要围绕行动来构思问题。比如他会重新设问：不采取行动的代价是什么？这对我来说非常有效，它让我清晰地看到了自己当前处境中存在的诸多代价。（00:41:16）：所以实际上，我想感谢你。有趣的是，你在我听你参加的播客时给我发了消息。我记得那期节目是和大卫·佩雷尔（David Perell）一起的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, I slid into your DMs.
turns.zh: 是啊，我私信你了。

turns.speaker: Paul Millerd
turns.en: But I was listening to your podcast and you were talking about hiring a community manager. And this is actually something I've done in the past few weeks. And I think I was scared to commit to the community because I didn't want to create a job for myself. (00:41:48): And one thing I've realized is that I'm scared of creating a job for myself, but I sort of reframed the cost of inaction. What's the cost of inaction is if I don't actually hire someone, I'm going to drain all my creative energy, and that's an existential risk to this path. And so that's one example of I'm always thinking about these things, and that enabled me to take very quick action on that. (00:42:17): But I think it was helpful to hear from you. You were like, "I'm not a community manager." And this is a big aha for me, because I launched my community at the beginning of this year. I suck at community management. I'm not good at it, but I found somebody that actually was good at it and I was like, "There are people that like this and are good at it." So that's one thing. I think more broadly though is some fears don't disappear. So that's a very specific project-based fear. (00:42:47): Existential fears around health, death, importance, money, they don't really go away. I think the great thing about this path for me is that you can't pretend like they don't exist. They sort of just punch you in the face. You'll wake up one day and you'll have an existential breakdown of, "What the heck am I doing? Is this sustainable? This is so silly. Am I going to run out of money? Next year, are my book sales going to tank?" And so the longer I've been on this path, those big worries turn into these small little daily things that pop up. And I'll sort of have a conversation with my fear and I'll say, "We're worrying about money today. Okay, I see you. Yeah, that's real. Yeah, I don't know if we can solve that, but yeah, six and a half years, let's keep going. Let's see if it works." (00:43:48): Yeah, that's the thing that makes me feel better every time something like that comes up is, it's worked this long. It's probably going to work for a lot longer. There's this concept of [inaudible 00:43:56], of the time something is going to last is usually as long as it's already lasted. And so that always makes me feel better. The main thing I think about, is am I going to run out of stuff with a newsletter to write about? And it's been four years now. I'm like, "Nah, it's probably going to keep going for at least four more years." (00:44:12): It's very important to dance with your fears and really get in with them. If I'm afraid of not making money, it's very reasonable that book sales will fall. And so I don't know if we can sustain our lifestyle on what I have set up two, three years down the road. But taking that fear and saying, "Okay, I'm going to solve that and make that fear go away by getting a job," is off the table. So I have no choice but to actually just be like, "Yeah, that fear's going to be here. It's going to be part of my life, and we're going to have to just deal with it."
turns.zh:
可是我当时在听你的播客，你提到要招聘一名社区经理。这实际上是我过去几周一直在做的事。我觉得自己一直不敢投身社区管理，就是因为不想给自己创造一份工作。（00:41:48）：后来我意识到，尽管害怕为自己创造工作机会，但我重新审视了不作为的代价。若不招聘社区经理，我会耗尽所有创造力，这对我的事业发展将是致命威胁。这就是我时刻反思这些问题的例子，它帮助我迅速采取行动。

（00:42:17）：不过听你讲话对我很有启发。你说"我不是社区经理"。这对我来说是个重要的顿悟，因为今年初我刚启动自己的社区项目。我的社区管理能力很差，但我找到了真正擅长这方面的人，这让我意识到确实有人热爱并擅长这项工作。当然，更深层的恐惧——比如健康、死亡、自我价值、金钱等——永远挥之不去。我认为这条道路的妙处在于，你无法假装它们不存在。它们会突然给你一记重击。某天你会突然陷入自我怀疑："我到底在做什么？这能持续下去吗？太荒谬了！明年书销量会暴跌吗？"随着时间推移，这些大恐惧会演变成日常琐事。我会和恐惧对话："今天担心钱的问题？好吧，我明白了。是的，我不知道能否解决，但六年半坚持下来了，继续吧，看看结果如何。"

（00:43:48）：每次面对这些担忧时，最能安慰我的是："到目前为止这条路走得通，未来很可能也会持续下去。"正如[此处缺失]所言，事情能持续多久往往取决于它已经持续了多久。这总能让我安心。现在我最担心的就是，四年后写时事通讯会没有素材了。但四年过去了，我想："不会的，至少还能再写四年。"

（00:44:12）：与恐惧共舞、直面它们至关重要。若害怕书销量下滑，那确实合理。但我不确定未来两三年能否靠现有模式维持生活。但把恐惧归咎于"找份工作就能解决"，这条路走不通。我别无选择，只能坦然接受："好吧，这些恐惧会伴随我一生，我们必须应对它们。"

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Along those lines, is there a path you took that was a big failure or didn't work out, something that you thought was going to be a big opportunity and wasn't?
turns.zh: 顺着这个思路，有没有哪条你走过的路失败了，或者没有达到预期？有没有你曾认为是重大机遇却落空的项目？

turns.speaker: Paul Millerd
turns.en: The first 10 years of my career, I just kept jumping from job to job. I think I was looking for my current path in job shaped containers and I couldn't find it. And I was just so desperate to find a really good situation. (00:45:15): And there were all sorts of circumstances, like bosses who hired me, kept quitting immediately after I would join. Layoffs, all sorts of random things that happened that were very weird. And I just sort of kept searching.
turns.zh: 职业生涯的前十年，我一直在不断换工作。当时我想，我是在用一份份工作来寻找自己如今的道路，却始终未能如愿。我当时特别渴望找到一份理想的工作环境。（00:45:15）各种状况接踵而至，比如雇主聘用我后又立刻离职，裁员，还有各种奇怪的突发状况。我只能不断探索。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So I've been comfortable with trying things, and starting new things, and experimenting for a long time. And so one frame I have, I call it ship, quit, and learn, which is what is the quickest way I can ship something designed to quit, but as soon as I ship it, I learn about what to do next?
turns.zh: 所以我一直很习惯尝试新事物、开启新项目并不断探索。我的一个思维框架叫“上线、退出、学习”，即如何最快速地完成某个项目，然后退出。但一旦项目完成，我又能学到下一步该做什么。

turns.speaker: Paul Millerd
turns.en: And so this is how I started my podcast. I just said, "I'm going to do five episodes." I stole this from Tim Ferriss as well. I'm going to do five episodes. I'm going to see how it feels. And this is one of these things, super energizing. I love how I feel after podcast conversations. I'm going to keep doing it. I wasn't aiming at success, but it was like, "I know I can keep doing the podcast and my newsletter." I had that experience, that feeling from it, but there are things I've tried that I'm like, "Yeah, not again." A couple consulting and advisory type things early on in my path, it was like, "Whoa, I need to build in protectors such that I don't take a gig like this again."
turns.zh: 这就是我开播播客的初衷。我就想：“我先做五期试试看。” 这个想法也是从蒂姆·费里斯那里借鉴来的。先做五期试试，看看感觉如何。这件事特别能激发动力。我喜欢播客后那种充实的感觉，所以决定坚持下去。我原本没想追求成功，只是觉得：“我能继续做播客和通讯。” 但有些尝试让我打了退堂鼓。比如早期尝试的咨询顾问类项目，我当时就想：“得赶紧设置保护机制，不能再接这种活儿了。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I connect to something you said earlier, which I super resonate with, which is you want to avoid creating jobs for yourself that you don't enjoy with this path. There's so many things you could be doing and so many pulls that often, for me, it's like writing a book is always this thing that's out there. Actually, starting a podcast with one of these for a long time, "I don't want to start a podcast. Life is good. I got this awesome newsletter. Things are going great. Why would I want more work?" (00:47:05): Eventually I crumbled, and I did it, and here we are, and I'm happy I did. But there's all these other things that are always like, "I should do these things." But I think it's really important to pay attention to what do you not enjoy and don't do that. It's easy to create bad jobs for yourself. (00:47:19): A really clear example of that is finding a niche that you don't enjoy, spending time on in this life of writing about something you don't actually care about, or podcasting about something you don't care about. You just created a job for yourself you hate. Why would you do that? And so it comes back to paying attention to what gives you energy.
turns.zh: 你之前提到要避免为自己创造不喜欢的工作，太有共鸣了。总有各种诱惑，但对我来说，写书这件事始终在召唤。其实很早就有做播客的念头，但总想：“我不想做播客。生活挺好的，我有这么棒的通讯，事情进展顺利，为啥还要多一份工作？” （00:47:05）最后我还是妥协了，现在回头很庆幸。但还有很多事总在诱惑你：“你应该做这个。” 关键是注意哪些事让你不开心，就别做。很容易给自己创造糟糕的工作环境。（00:47:19）最明显的例子就是找个自己不喜欢的细分领域，花时间写自己不感兴趣的内容，或者做不感兴趣的播客。就是给自己创造一份讨厌的工作，为什么要这么做？所以关键还是关注能给你能量的方向。

turns.speaker: Paul Millerd
turns.en: So I've created a lot of slack in my life. So I'd say 95% of my days, I cannot work. So I don't do meetings. I don't really have employees or anything like that. I have contractors, but I hire contractors for very specific roles. And I create systems such that we can do it asynchronously. And of course, I'll have conversations with them if they want to jump on a call. But I optimize for people that want asynchronous and work on those specific things. So I'm just very conscious of that. (00:48:15): I think one challenge I have now is I've created so many things that I'm doing a few things really well, and then sort of ignoring a lot of them. So I actually feel like I'm in this evolution right now of trying to figure out what comes next. (00:48:35): So we haven't even talked about this, but I started this business strategy early on in my path because I wanted to productize my consulting. And one of the consulting projects I loved early on was training people on consulting skills. I did a training program for a consulting firm in Boston, and I was like, "Ooh, I could turn this into an online course." And that has slowly built and evolved, and I do workshops now with companies. And that made most of my money from years two to five when I started moving away from project-based consulting. (00:49:13): And so the game I was playing was make money from that, don't focus on it too much, spend minimal time, don't try to maximize for success. Create a self-paced course, because I am not interested in making more money in a cohort-based course, because I just don't want to spend the time. And then use all the abundant time to write and explore, create podcasts, spend time with my wife, and do all the non-work experiments, see how I feel and write about it. (00:49:44): Now I'm making money from the work I love, which is very weird. I'm going to make, I'll hit soon about $200,000 made for my book, which is mind-blowing. I published a book completely on my terms about what I love and loved the process of it. It's so crazy.
turns.zh: 于是，我在生活中留出了大量空闲时间。可以说，我95%的时间都无法工作。因此，我不会参加会议，也没有雇员之类的人。我有承包商，但只雇佣他们负责特定任务。我还建立了系统，确保工作可以异步进行。当然，如果他们想通话，我也会和他们沟通。但我优先考虑那些希望异步工作、专注于特定任务的人。这是我一直很注意的地方。（00:48:15）：我现在面临的一个挑战是，我创建了太多项目，有些做得很好，但很多却被忽视了。所以我现在正处于一个进化阶段，试图弄清楚下一步该怎么做。（00:48:35）：虽然我们还没聊到这一点，但我在职业生涯早期就开始规划商业策略，因为我想将咨询服务产品化。早期我很喜欢的一个咨询项目是培训咨询技能。我为波士顿一家咨询公司设计了一个培训项目，当时我就想：“哇，我可以把这个做成在线课程。”这个项目逐渐发展壮大，现在我为企业提供研讨会。在远离项目式咨询的第二到第五年间，我的大部分收入都来自这个项目。（00:49:13）：所以我的策略是从中赚钱，但不投入太多精力，尽量减少时间投入，不追求成功最大化。创建自学课程，因为我对批量课程赚钱不感兴趣，因为我不想花那个时间。然后利用大量空闲时间写作、探索、制作播客、陪妻子，以及进行各种非工作实验，观察感受并记录下来。（00:49:44）：现在我靠自己热爱的工作赚钱，这感觉太奇妙了。我的书收入很快就要达到20万美元了，简直令人惊叹。我完全按照自己的方式出版了一本关于热爱之事的书，并且乐在其中。这太不可思议了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's amazing.
turns.zh: 太棒了。

turns.speaker: Paul Millerd
turns.en: And so now I'm building a community around that. That's really fun. I'm doing the podcast. I have some sponsors around that. And so that's sort of taking over. I still have this StrategyU though. (00:50:19): So now I'm trying to figure out how to unwind some of these things. I'm actually exploring trying to find somebody that might want to start their own pathless path, like a strategy consultant that wants to leave that world, that wants to be an operator on this business. So if you're listening, I've recently come to terms with this might be the path forward. (00:50:38): But yeah, it's a constant journey of protecting your time, creating that space, going down projects you want to execute, but then stepping back and like, "Okay, I have all this maintenance I'm doing. How do I outsource this, eliminate it, restart, recreate?" And I think this path is really just a commitment to constant reinvention, which is really, really hard. And you shouldn't do it unless you get some satisfaction out of personal reflection and that journey.
turns.zh: 现在我正围绕这个方向建立一个社区。这真的很有趣。我在做播客，也有一些赞助商。现在这个项目越来越占据主导地位。不过我还是保留了StrategyU这个项目。（00:50:19）：所以现在我在试图理清如何简化这些事务。我正在探索是否能找到愿意开辟自己“无路之路”的人——比如想离开咨询行业、转做商业运营的策略顾问。如果你正在听，我最近意识到这或许是未来的发展方向。（00:50:38）：但没错，这是一条不断保护时间、创造空间、推进想做项目的旅程，然后退后一步，问：“好吧，我现在有很多维护工作要做。如何外包、消除、重启、重建？”我认为这条路其实就是不断自我革新的承诺，而这真的非常非常难。除非你能从个人反思和这段旅程中获得满足感，否则不该走这条路。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: For someone that may want to help you with that program, what's the best way to reach out to you if they're just like, "Oh shit, this is a cool opportunity"?
turns.zh: 对于那些可能想参与这个项目的人，如果他们只是想说：“天哪，这真是个绝佳的机会！”该如何联系你呢？

turns.speaker: Paul Millerd
turns.en: Yeah, Twitter, paul@strategyu.co, or I'm very easy to find. My email is all over the place. But yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊，推特账号是paul@strategyu.co，找我也很容易。我的邮箱到处都是。不过确实如此。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: We'll link to it in the show notes too. Just a couple more questions. I feel like one criticism of this path is, is there anyone left to actually do work at companies and build things and scale if everyone ends up being on this pathless path, creating content, starting their own companies? Do you have any thoughts on that side of things?
turns.zh: 我们也会在节目笔记中附上链接。再问几个问题。我觉得对这条路的批评之一是，如果每个人都走上这条无路可走的路——创作内容、创办自己的公司——那公司里还能剩下谁去实际工作、开发产品、推动业务扩张呢？你对此有什么看法？

turns.speaker: Paul Millerd
turns.en: I don't buy that, because I've met most people and most people are like, "Hell no," when they hear about my life. (00:51:51): I think it's an interesting critique. I also think there's a more secular trend of gigification of work. All the growth in the economy from 2005 to 2015 in the labor market came from alternative work arrangements. So if you search David Deming's work on this, it's pretty compelling. Right now, we don't really count non-traditional work that well, so it's really hard to get good data on this. But even the way companies are treating their internal talent, it's much more project-based. People are shifting around, moving to different roles a lot quicker. And I think that's going to continue. (00:52:29): So you could make an argument that people will actually be able to slot into companies more easily in the future. Right now, companies under exploit the creator economy and the freelance economy, because they're so tied to you have to hire somebody through a full-time job. (00:52:47): So I think there's two sides to that, is one, most people would hate my life. And two, the world is becoming more giggified. So it could go back the other way actually.
turns.zh: 我不认同这种观点，因为我见过大多数人。当他们听说我的生活时，都会说“绝不可能”。（00:51:51）我认为这是一个有趣的批评。我还认为，有一种更普遍的趋势是工作模式的零工化。从2005年到2015年，劳动力市场的经济增长主要来自非传统的工作安排。所以如果你查阅大卫·德明（David Deming）关于这一点的研究，数据相当有说服力。目前，我们对非传统工作的统计数据做得不够好，所以很难获取准确数据。但即使是公司内部对人才的管理方式，也越来越以项目为导向了。人们换岗、转换角色变得更加频繁。我认为这种趋势会持续下去。（00:52:29）所以可以说，未来人们进入公司会更容易。目前，公司对创作者经济和自由职业经济的利用率很低，因为它们太受制于必须通过全职工作雇佣人才的模式了。（00:52:47）所以我认为这有两个方面：一是大多数人会讨厌我的生活；二是世界正在变得更加零工化。所以情况可能还会反过来。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I really like that advice. Paul, is there anything else you want to leave listeners with to maybe start down this pathless path or any other piece of advice before we get to very exciting lightning round?
turns.zh: 我真的很喜欢这个建议。保罗，还有什么想留给听众的建议，让他们或许能踏上这条无路可走的道路，或者在我们进入激动人心的闪电问答环节之前的其他建议吗？

turns.speaker: Paul Millerd
turns.en: I think the key thing that doesn't get talked about enough is it might be hard and it might suck, but it might be worth it. And I think that's a hard reframe for people, because people will say, "Well, I'm worried about not knowing what I'll do or not making money and all these things." And it's like, yeah, I felt like after quitting my job. (00:53:44): But man, I'm so glad I did it, because it enabled me to now know that I don't have regrets about trying this and figuring it out. And a lot of people that do go back to their jobs are so much happier, because they know I tested that, I found my boundaries, I need more stability. It's not this quit your job and get rich pitch. It's very much like if you're somebody that has a sense that there's something more, there probably is, and it might be worth exploring.
turns.zh: 我认为最常被忽视的一点是，这条路可能会很艰难，也许会很糟糕，但它可能是值得的。这对人们来说是一个很难接受的转变，因为人们会说：“我担心不知道该做什么，或者赚不到钱，还有这些问题。”而我当时辞职后就感受到了这种恐惧。（00:53:44）但天哪，我真高兴自己这么做了，因为这让我现在知道，尝试这条路并摸索出来，我没有遗憾。很多回归职场的人都开心多了，因为他们知道我测试过界限，找到了自己的边界，知道自己需要更多稳定性。这不是那种辞职就能暴富的骗局。这更多的是，如果你有一种感觉觉得还有更多可能，那很可能确实有，而且值得探索。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's the next step you recommend someone take to start exploring this pathless path? What's something they could do today or tomorrow or in the next-
turns.zh: 你建议人们下一步该怎么做，才能开始探索这条无路可走的道路？他们今天、明天或者接下来几周可以做些什么？

turns.speaker: Paul Millerd
turns.en: Read my book.
turns.zh: 读我的书吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Perfect.
turns.zh: 好的。

turns.speaker: Paul Millerd
turns.en: So I'm very committed to creating resources for people around this. My podcast is all conversations of people on an unconventional path, and sort of the inner game of work. And I don't talk about tactics and outcomes as much as really just, how does it feel? How'd you deal with that? Things like that. And so I do that in my newsletter, my podcast, etc. But just find people that are on interesting pasts and ask them about their lives. (00:54:59): One interesting thing I've had happen to me over the past few years is I've just met a much more wider diversity of people. I'm friends with people that work at restaurants, and work part time, and work weird schedules, and work nine months of the year and take three months off. And now it just feels so much more normal what I'm doing, because before all I knew was full-time workers. I was working all the time, and that's all you're surrounded by. So yeah, try to find the weirdos.
turns.zh: 因此，我致力于为人们创造相关资源。我的播客全是那些走非传统道路的人的对谈，探讨工作的内在逻辑。我不常谈论策略和成果，而是更关注他们的真实感受和应对方式。比如：你当时是如何处理的？这些问题在我的新闻通讯和播客中反复出现。我会寻找那些有着独特过往经历的人，请他们分享自己的生活故事。（00:54:59）过去几年里，我遇到了形形色色的人。我结交了在餐馆工作的朋友，兼职员工，工作时间不规律的人，还有一年工作九个月、休息三个月的人。这让我意识到自己所做的事情变得更加平常，因为之前我只接触过全职工作者。我那时一直埋头工作，周围都是同类人。所以，是的，去寻找那些与众不同的人吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. And for folks that want to check out your book, should I just Google The Pathless Path?
turns.zh: 太棒了。如果有人想了解你的书，应该直接在谷歌上搜索《无路之路》吗？

turns.speaker: Paul Millerd
turns.en: Pathlesspath.com. I just moved over everything last month.
turns.zh: 网址是Pathlesspath.com。我上个月刚把所有内容迁移过去。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, great. And then we'll link to all of these things in the show notes. With that Paul, we've reached our very exciting lightning round. Are you ready?
turns.zh: 好的，太棒了。我们会在节目笔记中附上所有链接。保罗，现在到了我们激动人心的闪电问答环节。你准备好了吗？

turns.speaker: Paul Millerd
turns.en: I am ready.
turns.zh: 我已经准备好了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What are two or three books that you've recommended most to other people?
turns.zh: 你向他人推荐最多的两三本书是什么？

turns.speaker: Paul Millerd
turns.en: Yeah, one is called The Great Work of Your Life. Sounds like a cheesy title, but that's actually a good resource for people that want to hear about people from history. Over the past several hundred years, different eras of people that really did design their life around work. It was really interesting, and that was a great book. (00:56:16): A second book I'd recommend, I actually really like Luke Burgis' book Wanting. That was another great personal story/deep dive into a nerdy topic. That's my favorite kind of book. That's the kind of book I wrote, which was personal memoir plus nerdy deep dive. And Luke Burgis' is really good too, more from a tech perspective, because he went down the startup path as well. Tut that's a great book. That was my favorite read of the year.
turns.zh: 是啊，其中一本叫《你人生的伟大事业》。听起来是个俗气的书名，但对那些想了解历史人物的人来说，这确实是个好资源。过去几百年间，不同时代的人确实围绕工作设计了自己的生活。这本书真的很有趣，也是我最喜欢的书。（00:56:16）我还推荐卢克·伯吉斯的《渴望》。这是另一本很棒的个人故事/深度探讨书籍，属于我最爱的类型。这本书我写的也是这种风格，既是个人回忆录，又对某个领域进行了深度探讨。卢克·伯吉斯的书也很棒，从科技视角出发，因为他也走过创业之路。这本书很棒，是我今年最喜欢的读物。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What is a favorite recent movie or TV show?
turns.zh: 最近你最喜欢的电影或电视剧是什么？

turns.speaker: Paul Millerd
turns.en: I struggle to answer this, because I'm not watching much TV. I did watch the Anthony Bourdain documentary. That was excellent. Talk about a pathless path, and the ups and downs, and the struggles, and the dark side of it. Man, that person was bringing forth what is inside of him and grappling with his demons at the same time. That was a powerful story worth watching.
turns.zh: 这个问题我很难回答，因为我不怎么看电视。不过我看过安东尼·波登的纪录片。太棒了。讲的就是无路之路，以及其中的起起落落和挣扎，还有黑暗面。这人把内心的挣扎和恶魔同时呈现出来，真是个震撼人心的故事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Do you have a favorite interview question that you like to ask when you interview, say, contractors or anyone else you work with or hire?
turns.zh: 在面试承包商或其他合作伙伴时，你最喜欢问的一个问题是什么？

turns.speaker: Paul Millerd
turns.en: I'm always curious about, what makes you come alive? I want to work with people that are alive, and connected, and inspired. So the two people I'm working with right now, one's a podcast producer in Poland, but he's doing a bunch of other stuff around video. And he's super energized, used to be a lawyer, reinventing himself. The other person is also a former finance person in India, and she's two years into this self-employment journey. She's writing and exploring all these ideas. So yeah, I'm always looking for that energy first and skills second.
turns.zh: 我总是很好奇，什么能激发你的活力？我希望与那些充满活力、相互联结、富有灵感的人共事。所以我现在合作的两位，一位是波兰的播客制作人，但他还在做其他视频相关的工作。他精力充沛，曾是一名律师，现在正重塑自我。另一位是印度的前金融从业者，她已经踏上自我创业之路两年了。她不断写作，探索各种创意。所以是的，我首先寻找这种活力，然后才是技能。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there a favorite product you've recently discovered that you love?
turns.zh: 最近有没有发现特别喜欢的产品？

turns.speaker: Paul Millerd
turns.en: I really love the Nuna travel stroller. Super convenient for traveling.
turns.zh: 我真的很喜欢Nuna旅行婴儿车。出差旅行时超级方便。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: We don't have the travel stroller, but we have the Nuna car seat.
turns.zh: 我们没有旅行婴儿车，但有Nuna儿童座椅。

turns.speaker: Paul Millerd
turns.en: Yeah, yeah, we have that one too. It fits. So we've brought that around the world. That's been super convenient. And then more on the tech side, I just got into the esim game. That was amazing. And then ChatGPT, I just created my own GPT to do podcast show notes automatically for me today. Took me an hour to train it, and it is incredible, so that's amazing.
turns.zh: 对，我们也有那个。很合适。我们带着它环游了世界，真的很方便。技术方面的话，我刚接触了eSIM服务。太棒了。还有ChatGPT，我今天用它自动为播客生成节目笔记。花了一个小时训练它，效果令人惊叹。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's awesome. I don't know if folks know, but there's a lennybot.com site that uses all of my podcast transcripts and newsletter to have a little bot that you could ask questions to. That's working actually, shockingly well. We're going to try using the new GPT thing that they just launched, where you can kind of train your own GPT and that'll be fun. And actually, a podcast listener reached out to me and offered to help build this thing, so that's a huge success story from this podcast. (00:59:12): Next question, two more questions. Do you have a favorite life motto that you find yourself coming back to, sharing with friends, finding really useful in work or in life?
turns.zh: 太棒了。不知道大家是否知道，lennybot.com这个网站会用我所有的播客文字记录和新闻通讯来训练一个小机器人，你可以向它提问。效果出奇地好。我们打算试试他们刚推出的新GPT功能，可以自己训练专属GPT，应该会很有趣。实际上，有位播客听众主动联系我，提出帮忙开发这个功能，这真是这个播客的一个巨大成功。（00:59:12）：最后两个问题。你有没有最喜欢的座右铭，经常回想、与朋友分享、在工作或生活中觉得特别有用的？

turns.speaker: Paul Millerd
turns.en: One, coming alive over getting ahead. That's something I keep coming back to. I'm default skeptical of chasing achievement, and I use this to remind myself that it is about that personal energy versus extrinsic outcomes. (00:59:43): I'm very convinced from my own life experience that the extrinsic outcomes aren't going to do a ton for me. Sure, I need to make enough money. But when I'm in extended states of feeling alive and connected to everything I'm doing in my life, that's it. And I basically repeated this mantra to myself right before rejecting the book deal. It was like I did not feel good in the conversation with the people. They talked down to me, they told me that I probably wouldn't succeed, and it was like coming alive over getting ahead. Don't need their prestige.
turns.zh: 第一条，活力胜于追逐成功。这是我反复回味的理念。我对追求成就持默认怀疑态度，我用这句话提醒自己，关键在于个人能量而非外在成果。（00:59:43）：从我自己的生活经验来看，我深信外在成果对我的意义不大。当然，我需要赚足够的钱。但当我长期处于充满活力、与生活紧密相连的状态时，那才是关键。在拒绝那份书约前，我反复对自己说这句话。当时和对方交谈时，我感觉很不自在。他们贬低我，告诉我可能不会成功，但我坚持活力胜于追逐成功。不需要他们的虚名。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Final question. You've been podcasting, I think, for six years. What's your best piece of advice for someone that wants to start podcasting, has maybe already been doing podcasting like myself, or being successful or anything along those lines?
turns.zh: 最后一个问题。你做播客已经六年了，对于想开始做播客、像我一样已经在做播客或者已经取得成功的人，你有什么最佳建议？

turns.speaker: Paul Millerd
turns.en: Yeah. I think if you want to podcast to make money, it's probably not something you should get into. Even if you have an audience, it's probably not the best way. I think if you have a massive audience, it can work, but it takes a really long time. Podcast is the ultimate long game, so you need to find some intrinsic connection to what you're actually doing. If you don't love the conversations or the format you're doing, don't do it. (01:01:05): But yeah, I would recommend more people start podcasts. I'm against... The New York Times says there's too many podcasts, but I take the opposing view. I don't think there's that many podcasts. If you ask people in their personal life out of tech bubbles, "How many people in your life have a podcast?" Now in Austin, a lot of people have podcasts, but yeah, most people don't have a podcast. Even if you do something like interview your parents or anything, it's such a cool, creative thing. It's free. It's free, and you can send it to everyone in the world. Podcasts and newsletters are incredible innovations. Let it rip. You had to get permission to do these things 10, 15 years ago. It's so great to be alive in today's world.
turns.zh: 是啊。我觉得如果你想靠播客赚钱，那可能不值得尝试。即便你已经积累了一批听众，这也不是最佳途径。我认为如果你拥有庞大的听众群体，或许能成功，但这需要耗费极长的时间。播客是一项需要长期积累的项目，所以你必须对自己所做之事怀有内在的热忱。如果你不热爱你所进行的对话或播客形式，那就别做了。（01:01:05）不过是的，我还是建议更多人开始做播客。我反对《纽约时报》所说的播客数量过多这一观点，但我持相反立场。我认为播客的数量并不多。如果你问那些不熟悉科技圈的人，他们的生活中有多少人听播客？现在在奥斯汀，很多人都做播客，但大多数人其实不听。即便你做些采访父母之类的节目，这也是件很酷、很有创意的事。它是免费的，你可以把内容分享给全世界的人。播客和新闻通讯都是了不起的创新成果。尽情发挥吧。在10到15年前，你做这些事还得获得许可。生活在当今世界真是太棒了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I feel like when people say there's too much of say newsletters, too many podcasts, my answer is always there's always room for better newsletters and better podcasts. If you can deliver more useful, valuable, interesting stuff, people are going to pay attention. The bar just keeps rising is the challenge.
turns.zh: 我觉得当人们说新闻通讯或播客太多时，我的回答永远是，总有提升空间。只要你能提供更有用、更有价值、更有趣的内容，人们就会关注。挑战就在于标准不断提高。

turns.speaker: Paul Millerd
turns.en: Yeah. It's also like do it for the sake of itself. Do it for the creative act. The creative act can be super meaningful in and of itself. I've lost money in my podcast over the lifetime of it. Love it. I don't care. I'm going to keep doing it.
turns.zh: 是啊。你也可以为了热爱而做这件事。为了创作而创作。创作本身就可能意义非凡。我做播客这么多年，一直在亏钱。但我热爱它，我不在乎。我会继续做下去。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And also, the best stuff often comes from just doing it for yourself and then realizing, "Wow, other people might find this interesting."
turns.zh: 而且，最棒的内容往往源自你为自己而做，然后突然发现：“哇，其他人可能也会觉得这很有趣。”

turns.speaker: Paul Millerd
turns.en: Yeah. I didn't start getting podcast feedback until the last two years when it started growing a lot more. I was sort of just doing it into the void.
turns.zh: 是啊。我直到最近两年播客开始发展得更快时，才开始收到反馈。在此之前，我一直是默默做事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Speaking of that, Paul, we've been on our own pathless path. I feel like we're going to send a number of folks on their pathless path. Two final questions. Where can folks find you online if they want to reach out and learn more about what you're sharing in your journey, and how can listeners be useful to you?
turns.zh: 说到这，保罗，我们一直在走自己的“无路之路”。我觉得我们会引导许多人踏上他们自己的“无路之路”。最后两个问题。如果有人想了解更多你的旅程，可以在哪里找到你？听众如何能为你提供帮助？

turns.speaker: Paul Millerd
turns.en: Yeah, so I've been compiling a lot of my more recent stuff under pathlesspath.com, that will link you to my podcast, newsletter, community, and book. And I'm always willing to gift my book to anyone in the world who wants it. Just email me. I'll even send you a printed copy, if you don't have the money to do it. And I'm always happy to send bulk orders to people that want to gift it and do book clubs or things like that. And happy to send it at the author rate, which is about $4 per book. (01:03:34): And yeah, I am starting to explore the potential of selling my StrategyU business or finding an owner operator who might want to get some sort of profit sharing or something like that. It'd be interesting if there are former consultants that might be interested in something like that. (01:03:54): I don't know. I'm so bad at asking for help. I think if you want to share my book, that would be cool, because it is pretty neat to make money doing something from something I'm really proud of.
turns.zh:
是的，我一直在pathlesspath.com上整理我最近的很多内容，这个网站会链接到我的播客、新闻通讯、社区和书籍。如果世界上有任何人想要这本书，我都乐意赠送。只需给我发邮件即可。如果你没有钱购买，我甚至可以寄给你印刷版。我也很乐意为想要赠送书籍、举办读书会等活动的人批量提供书籍，并且可以按照作者价格出售，每本约4美元。  
（01:03:34）是的，我开始探索出售StrategyU业务的可能性，或者寻找一位所有者经营者，他可能希望获得某种利润分成之类的安排。如果有前顾问对此感兴趣，那会很有趣。  
（01:03:54）我不知道。我不太善于寻求帮助。我觉得如果你想分享我的书，那就太好了。因为用我真正引以为傲的东西赚钱，这感觉很棒。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Go buy The Pathless Path, available all online bookstores, I imagine. Paul, thank you so much for being here.
turns.zh: 去买《无路之路》吧，我想所有在线书店都有售。保罗，非常感谢你能来。

turns.speaker: Paul Millerd
turns.en: Amazing. Keep going on your path too. I'm really inspired by how you're approaching your path and sharing your reflections too.
turns.zh: 太棒了。你也要继续走自己的路。我真的很受启发，你处理人生道路的方式以及分享自己的思考都让我深受触动。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I appreciate that. Bye everyone.
turns.zh: 非常感谢。大家再见。

turns.speaker: Paul Millerd
turns.en: Adios.
